thesis: A person retains review of a delegated task only if relevant reasons can reach that person with adequate reliability, usability and timeliness when the recommendation process makes the particular error being reviewed. The strongest version is a necessary condition for an assigned review function, not a requirement of complete independence, unaided competence, universal human veto or guaranteed correction. Under ‘Why the route matters,’ the decisive claim is: ‘she can see the request only if the program has already decided not to dismiss it.’ Authority to reject therefore does not establish the capacity to review that dismissal.
claimed_contribution: Under ‘What the existing accounts already establish,’ the manuscript expressly disclaims discovering the inadequacy of override. Its proposed refinements are that ‘the route to the reviewer remains adequate under the error being reviewed’ and that adequacy depends on whether review concerns an individual result or an ongoing practice. It connects these requirements to a particular person's continuing power, while allowing extensive delegation and checks within one product.

findings.manuscript_location: ‘What the existing accounts already establish’: ‘My proposed refinement concerns the particular failure that a review is supposed to catch’; ‘Why the route matters’: ‘A fixed inbox that displays every staff message can remain useful when a nearby recommendation model misclassifies one.’
findings.claim: The central safeguard has a substantially closer, uncited predecessor than the literature comparison acknowledges.
findings.analysis: Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens distinguish highlighting from filtering because the former preserves original information (§III.A, p. 288). They then permit extensive information automation conditional on access to raw data when its algorithms can be inappropriate (§IV.B.1, p. 292). This anticipates both the safeguard and its failure rationale, rather than merely warning about deskilling. The demonstrated problem is incomplete novelty positioning, not a refutation. [Primary text](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/11596569_A_model_for_types_and_levels_of_human_interaction_with_automation).
findings.effect_on_conclusion: Preserving access around filtering errors cannot itself establish novelty. The argument about an assigned reviewer's power remains available.
findings.repair_conditions: Compare this predecessor and explain what the philosophical necessity argument adds to its design recommendation.

findings.manuscript_location: ‘What the existing accounts already establish’: ‘whether the person is reviewing an individual result or the practice over time’; ‘Why the route matters’: ‘It is control over an ongoing practice, however, not an opportunity to correct every schedule before publication.’
findings.claim: The distinction between individual and process review is already explicit in uncited reviewability literature.
findings.analysis: Cobbe, Lee and Singh provide a framework for contextually appropriate evidence supporting both individual-decision review and assessment of the whole process. Section 3.2 also makes informational requirements relative to the accountability relationship. The manuscript's distinction is sound, but is not independently new. Its specific application to sampling and timely scheduling appeals is a further application. [Primary text](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.04201).
findings.effect_on_conclusion: The claimed contribution should narrow to applying this established distinction within the proposed dependence test.
findings.repair_conditions: Acknowledge reviewability literature and distinguish the manuscript's particular application from the established distinction.

findings.manuscript_location: ‘Why the route matters’: ‘The relevant independence is independence from the error being checked, not a count of companies, interfaces, or devices.’
findings.claim: A recent public draft closely overlaps this formulation, but its priority relative to the manuscript cannot be established.
findings.analysis: ER-018 expressly distinguishes evidential independence from numbers of reviewers or models and proposes checks targeted to consequential errors. Its page reports publication on 21 October 2026 and revision on 26 October. This is verified conceptual overlap, but the supplied manuscript has no composition or freeze date. Consequently, I cannot classify this document as demonstrably earlier than the manuscript. [Public draft](https://londonresearchcentreformarketingai.org.uk/research/024-offloading-human-oversight).
findings.effect_on_conclusion: Priority for this particular formulation remains unresolved; the older overlaps in L1 and L2 do not depend on this draft.
findings.repair_conditions: Compare the arguments if chronologically applicable, without inferring borrowing or priority from resemblance.

surviving_contribution: What survives is a philosophical synthesis and specification of an established oversight problem. Under ‘A power that lacks its occasion,’ ‘Control through review involves being able to change course for a reason’ connects information access to an individual's practical power. The matched theatre cases isolate this dependence while holding authority and competence fixed. ‘The strongest objection: all judgment depends on something’ then limits the requirement to a specified failure rather than complete independence. The sources examined do not establish that this entire argument, with its exact personal and task-relative scope, has already been made. Nevertheless, substantial components of the proposed refinements are prior results, so a claim to a newly discovered safeguard is unavailable. The major concern concerns substantiation of novelty, not fabricated citations or a demonstrated failure of the central necessary-condition argument.
remaining_questions: Under ‘What the existing accounts already establish,’ ‘A test of relevant failures therefore develops their approach’ leaves the precise increment open: is the contribution a new necessary condition, a practical specification of tracking, or a distinction between system-wide control and a particular person's assigned review power?

Under ‘Why the route matters,’ ‘The required reliability depends on the stakes, time available, and kind of mistake’ identifies relevant variables but supplies no rule for settling adequacy. This is an acknowledged unfinished question, not a demonstrated defect; comparison with operational oversight frameworks could clarify what the proposed test adds.

Under ‘The strongest objection: all judgment depends on something,’ the proposed omission test could be presented as an application of established failure testing. What additional philosophical claim, beyond such testing, follows from passing or failing it?
limitations: This was a finite public-web search across 21 queries, cited sources and selected adjacent literature. It does not establish exhaustive originality or the absence of closer predecessors.

The complete supplied manuscript, including its bibliography, was read. External sources were inspected at the locations recorded below; availability of a full text is not a claim that every page of that external work was read.

Bainbridge's publisher page returned 403, and the university-hosted copy was unavailable. Its original article was inspected through a public scan. A separate Crossref API request also failed, so the DOI registration record was not independently opened.

Pettit's author-hosted chapter exceeded the web tool's document-size limit. An older author URL and the publisher route also failed. Only its primary bibliographic record was opened; its substantive argument is not counted as independently verified.

Some failed retrievals were resolved through alternative copies: Parasuraman and colleagues and Kahl were read as displayed original texts on ResearchGate. Search snippets and related-publication panels were not treated as primary-text evidence.
The manuscript supplies no date permitting priority judgments against very recent 2026 publications. Publication dates reported by public pages do not establish intellectual influence.

The manuscript invokes no mathematical theorem or equation. The audit checked the scope of its formal-source attribution to Freiesleben and colleagues, not every proof or legal proposition in that preprint.

The theatre, mailbox, calculator and speech-software examples are presented as illustrations. They were not treated as documented events or empirical demonstrations that a particular deployed channel meets the proposed reliability threshold.

citation_audit.manuscript_location: ‘What the existing accounts already establish’: ‘People may lose the skills that they will later need for exceptional cases’; reference to §§1.1–2.1, pp. 775–777.
citation_audit.evidence: The original scan confirms author, title, year, journal, volume, issue and pages. The cited sections support skill deterioration, monitoring limitations and the problem of checking alarms or displays. The page range contains the relevant passages. Publisher and DOI-registration retrieval limitations are recorded separately.

citation_audit.manuscript_reference: Cohen and Suzor 2024, ‘Contesting the Public Interest in AI Governance.’
citation_audit.manuscript_location: ‘What the existing accounts already establish’: ‘an actor should not monopolize the information used to assess its conduct’ and ‘outside reviewers often must rely on internal records’; citation to §3.3.
citation_audit.evidence: The publisher confirms both authors, title, 2024 date, volume 13(3) and DOI. Section 3.3 supports both propositions. It also allows dependence on internal functions, so the manuscript correctly avoids attributing an absolute external-independence requirement.

citation_audit.manuscript_reference: Freiesleben, Meding, and König 2026, ‘Explainable AI Isn’t Enough! Rethinking Algorithmic Contestability.’
citation_audit.manuscript_location: ‘What the existing accounts already establish’: ‘distinguish changing one's circumstances to obtain a different result from challenging the result's correctness’; citation to §§1 and 5.3.
citation_audit.evidence: The exact v1 text and submission record confirm authors, title, identifier and 15 May 2026 date. Section 1 supports the distinction and the limited usefulness of standard explanations. Section 5.3 supports the additional-feature point. The manuscript does not claim that every explanation fails or import an unrestricted mathematical guarantee.

citation_audit.manuscript_reference: Santoni de Sio and van den Hoven 2018, ‘Meaningful Human Control over Autonomous Systems: A Philosophical Account.’
citation_audit.manuscript_location: ‘What the existing accounts already establish’: ‘Their tracking condition already asks how beliefs and actions would change with relevant facts, and allows reliability thresholds suited to the purpose’; citation to ‘Tracking’ and ‘Tracing.’
citation_audit.evidence: Publisher metadata matches the reference. The named sections support counterfactual responsiveness, purpose-relative reliability, distributed control, and the connection to human understanding and responsibility. The manuscript correctly states that the immediate operator's reasons need not be tracked in every circumstance.

citation_audit.manuscript_reference: Uncited illustrative cases and proposed test.
citation_audit.manuscript_location: ‘Why the route matters’: ‘A channel that delivers only one request in a million’; ‘The strongest objection: all judgment depends on something’: ‘One bounded test would deliberately omit requests from recommendations.’
citation_audit.evidence: These passages are explicitly illustrative or proposed, rather than reports of an experiment or deployment. No external quotation, numerical result or validation study is attributed to them. Their practical effectiveness is not established by the manuscript and was not inferred by this audit.
